newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Parliamentary UK learns US presidential politics.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Parliamentary UK learns US presidential politics.

text.p: Critics call it the "dumbing down" of Britain's election and blame the creeping influence of the presidential politics of the United States.

They deride the rise of personality at the expense of policy, the endless gossip over candidates' coiffure and wives, and the supreme importance of individual leaders over party policy in this, a parliamentary democracy.
Others shrug their shoulders -- with little to choose between the main parties in terms of policy, Britain has no option but to compare the men in the May 1 election and vote accordingly.

There is Prime Minister John Major: the grey man of British politics. Like Bob Dole, the failed Republican contender for the U.S. presidency, Major is portrayed as an experienced, if dull, pair of hands who can be trusted with the nation's well-being.
And there is Tony Blair, leader of the opposition Labour Party, a moderniser whose unswerving professionalism has earned him a tag for slickness.
Like Democrat President Bill Clinton, Blair has stolen the political centre ground and presents himself as a man of ideas, youth and vigour: ideal for these fast-changing times.
Voters say he is too packaged. Blair begs to differ.

"A lot of the so-called imagery and image-making is less relevant than people think," Blair said in a newspaper interview. "I'm not ignoring the personal side of politics but I don't think it will be a simple presidential campaign." Yet old-fashioned policy battles are hard to detect. Gone are the gaping divides about economics, nuclear weapons and common ownership, replaced by near consensus on the virtues of low inflation, personal responsibility and tough justice.
Never before has Britain -- where the prime minister is constitutionally accountable to parliament -- witnessed such a turn towards U.S. presidential-style politics.
"The British election gives me a sense of deja vu," Dick Morris, formerly a top adviser to Clinton, wrote in the Times.

"Ironically, at a time when American elections are fought more on the issue positions between parties -- the British model -- the Conservatives seem to want to move toward elections based on candidate personalities and credibility irrespective of party -- the American model," Morris said.
THE U.S INFLUENCE
Signs of Americanisation abound.

There are video link-ups between candidates and hand-picked "ordinary" voters who ask soft questions. Candidates board Clinton-style "battle buses" and hit the stump with smiling wives in tow, only to see their hemlines and hats picked over by the press. Blair's wife Cherie has already broken the British mould of political wives by holding down a high-powered job as a lawyer while raising a family and supporting her husband too.

Some Labour critics say that once in power, she might lead her husband further to the left and pull strings behind the scenes: the same criticism levelled at Clinton's wife Hillary, another high-powered lawyer-cum-mother.
Blair insists similarities between the Blairs and the Clintons, both young and highly succcessful families, do not mean the two political systems are one and the same.
"Well, our wives are both lawyers but there are a lot of them in the world. I am very happy to be compared to the president of the United States but I think the systems very different," Blair said.
Yet much else is imported from the United States.
SPIN DOCTORS
There is the rise of the so-called spin doctor and his invisible hand behind every media event, sound bite and policy.
Daily press conferences are planned for the Conservative prime minister to lend an air of authority and gravitas.
Labour and its U.S.-style rebuttal unit operate out of a state-of-the-art media centre to ensure they stay "on message".
Disgruntled party members grumble about a dictatorial trend in politics, saying policies are decreed from on high and leaked to the press rather than decided by consensus .
Most significantly, pundits say style increasingly swamps substance as ideological battles are replaced by beauty pageants between the men parading for top office.

Major and Blair both took centre stage at the launching of their party programmes, sidelining colleagues in what has traditionally been a group event. The leaders' pictures were plastered over the manifestos.

Unprecededented televised debates in a country proud of its tradition and parliamentary oratory are being discussed but seem unlikely because of arguments over how many party leaders should take part.

Should they go ahead, the debates are expected to highlight the different personalities on sale rather than shed light on policy. Major, after all, is far more popular than the rest of his party, which is trailing Labour by 20 points in the polls.
Conservatives reckon their best hope could be "Honest John" Major and his wife Norma, whose very ordinariness and aura of decency attract voters even if the party leaves them cold.

The same holds true for Labour. Blair may be regarded with suspicion -- voters call him smarmy, slick, too American -- but his is the face of New Labour and far more palatable to many undecided voters than the leftist Labour of old.
Whoever wins might face his toughest fight after the election, when presidential dreams must die.
For the next prime minister needs to win over a majority of members of parliament if he is to succeed in the job, not the spin doctors and strategists who helped send him there.
